newsitem.title: USA: WALL STREET WARMS TO CYCLICALS, SHUNS CONSUMERS.
newsitem.headline: WALL STREET WARMS TO CYCLICALS, SHUNS CONSUMERS.

text.p: Wall Street's love affair with consumer stocks and pharmaceuticals may be cooling off as the pace of economic activity continues strong and boosts the earnings of cyclical businesses such as forest products, chemicals, metals and automobiles.

"It appears that the economy is better than expected," said Richard Cripps, managing director at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "Stocks such as Coca-Cola Co or the drugs, normally viewed as defensive, are giving way to issues that are more cyclical in nature," he said.

Michael Metz, market strategist at Oppenheimer & Co, said investors are becoming disenchanted with stocks such as Coca-Cola and Gillette Co. He is skeptical that investors will continue to pay 30 or 40 times earnings for stocks whose revenue growth is in line with the underlying economy and whose profits are growing at a single-digit percentage rate.

Cripps said cyclicals are definitely the cheapest area of the market. He cited the case of General Motors Corp, trading at about eight times the 1997 consensus earnings forecast of $7.63 per share and 7.5 times the estimated earnings of $7.97 per share for 1998.
Opinions differ on the influence that the surging dollar will have on the earnings outlook for the multinationals.

The strong dollar, a high-flier before hitting a bit of a downdraft on Friday, causes profits earned overseas to be reduced when translated into U.S. currency. Metz said even if the dollar weakens a bit later in the year, the currency translation will still have a negative impact on year-over-year earnings comparisons.

Cripps said any problem with the dollar is overshadowed by the shift in money flows out of the defensive consumer stocks and into the cyclicals. He said the stock of Coca-Cola was weakening prior to last Thursday's announcement from the company that third-quarter earnings, including a gain from the sales of interests in two bottlers, would be only "slightly higher" than a year ago.
And he said the drug stocks were also losing steam prior to Monday's pronouncement from a Morgan Stanley analyst that the group should be afforded a "market weight" instead of an "overweight" rating.

As for financial stocks, Metz believes the sector will be hurt by higher interest rates accompanied by deterioration in credit quality. He expects long term rates to be closer to seven percent by the end of the year and does not believe the market has adjusted for higher rates.
The U.S. stock market overall is likely to be lower than today's levels at the end of the year and "perhaps painfully lower," Metz said.

Cripps believes by the end of the year the market averages may not be very different from their level now, but in the interim there could be a downward correction of some kind. He argues it would be better to ride it out with the cyclicals rather than the traditional defensive issues.
The Dow industrials closed up 31 to 8062 on Monday, rebounding from the the decline of 163 points for all of last week.
General Motors ended off 1-3/8 to 61-3/8, Gillette up 11/16 to 93-11/16 and Coca-Cola was off 15/16 to 61-3/4.
The 30-year Treasury bond was up slightly, with the yield at 6.63 percent.
